source: Park, Baek, Park, Lee (2026) Beyond One Path: Evaluating and Enhancing Divergent Thinking in Interactive LLM Agents (MUTATE, ReDNA)
finding: Closest test of a multi-step scaffold for divergence (gap 1). ReDNA splits Diverge (conditioned only on the scene and tools, goal and failure feedback withheld) from Narrowing (goal and failures reintroduced). It beat the ReAct base agent on GPT-5.4.
numbers: MUTATE: 10 scenarios, 56 mechanism-distinct paths, 8 frontier models; humans found 44.75/56 (79.9%) paths. Ablation on GPT-5.4: Base 27/56 (48.2%), Reflect-only 33/56 (58.9%), full ReDNA 38/56 (67.9%); originality 2.67 -> 2.77, elaboration 2.73 -> 3.26, groundedness 3.28 -> 3.72 (LLM judge). Open models weaker (Qwen3-30B 7/56 = 12.5%).
quote: divergence operate without convergence pressure before convergence reshapes the result
limits: Ten hand-built scenarios, LLM-as-judge (judge-human pairwise agreement 0.8447), no equal-token control reported; ReDNA uses extra calls, so gain may be partly compute. Not a pure DAT/AUT test.
agent_relevance: Direct support for an O-diverge step that is blind to the goal and to criticism, followed by a separate narrowing step. Needs an equal-token baseline in our own test.

source: Park et al. (2026) MUTATE, Section 5.3 and Appendix D.6: transfer of ReDNA to the Alternative Uses Test
finding: Same two-phase idea applied to AUT with GPT-5.4 raised judged originality and elaboration. Base made all uses in one call; ReDNA generated uses from the object alone, then a second call selected with the creativity criterion plus earlier uses.
numbers: AUT, T=0.7, mean of 3 runs per condition: originality 2.91 -> 3.77 (+0.86), elaboration 4.36 -> 4.97 (+0.61).
limits: One model, one temperature, 3 runs, LLM-judged, number of objects not stated in the main text; ReDNA makes 2 calls vs 1 so tokens are not matched; no fluency or diversity measure reported.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a two-call diverge-then-select scaffold lifts AUT originality, but the equal-token control (best-of-2 prompts) is still missing. Gap 1 only partly closed.

source: Zhang, Yu, Chong, Sicilia, Tomz, Manning, Shi (2026, v4) Verbalized Sampling: How to Mitigate Mode Collapse and Unlock LLM Diversity
finding: Controlled comparison at the same budget of N responses (Table 1): Direct, CoT, Sequence (k items per call), Multi-turn, VS-Standard, VS-CoT, VS-Multi. VS beat all of them on semantic diversity in poems, stories and jokes; VS-CoT and VS-Multi (which add step-by-step or multi-turn) gave the most diversity at high quality. Plain CoT was an instance-level baseline and did not match VS.
numbers: Creative writing diversity x1.6-2.1 over direct; human-rated diversity (1-4) poem 1.90 direct / 2.07 sequence / 2.39 VS; story 2.74 / 2.76 / 3.06; joke 1.83 / 2.93 / 3.01 (Prolific); human quality +25.7%; recovers 66.8% of base-model diversity; Tulu-70B diversity +182.6% vs direct after post-training; larger models gain 1.5-2x more than smaller ones; Sequence and VS-Standard lower quality but VS-CoT/VS-Multi do not.
limits: Tasks are poems, stories, jokes, dialogue and open QA, not AUT or DAT. Quality in poems measured with an automatic scorer. Diversity is embedding-based.
agent_relevance: Matched-budget evidence that a list-then-probability prompt plus a reasoning step is the strongest known cheap diverge operator. A best-of-N baseline is not in Table 1 (Direct with N calls is the nearest).

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Verbalized Sampling, Section 3 and Appendix D.2: typicality bias as cause of mode collapse
finding: Proposed cause of the Hivemind (gap 6): human raters prefer text that a base model finds likely, even when correctness is held equal. RLHF then sharpens the policy toward the base-model mode.
numbers: HelpSteer-v2 Bradley-Terry fit with base-model log-probability as predictor: Llama 3.1 405B beta 0.569 (SE 0.073, 6,874 tie-on-correctness pairs; odds ratio 1.42 per 1 SD; win prob +0.17 from -1 SD to +1 SD); GLM-4.5 beta 0.649 (OR 1.47, +0.19); adjusted slices beta 0.456 and 0.489 (28,283 pairs).
limits: Correlational, one preference dataset, base-model log-prob is only a proxy for typicality; length, readability and type-token controls shrink but keep the coefficient positive.
agent_relevance: Explains why temperature fails: the mode is in the aligned weights. Supports asking for a distribution (diverge many, then rank by low probability) instead of one answer.

source: Schaeffer, Miranda, Kazdan, Chudnovsky, Koyejo (2026) How Strong Is the Evidence for the Artificial Hivemind? Reevaluating Evidence for the Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models
finding: Critical re-analysis of the Hivemind paper (gaps 6 and 3). The 0.8 similarity threshold is tested against an undemanding null (responses to unrelated prompts). With a stricter null, a large share of pairs already exceed it, so much of the reported homogeneity is shared prompt geometry.
numbers: Median cosine of unrelated-prompt pairs 0.11; median for same-prompt, genuinely different ideas 0.723 (geometric clusters, 50 prompts) and 0.703 (LLM-labelled, 15 prompts); 20-32% of such pairs exceed 0.8. Hivemind same-prompt pairs exceed 0.8 about 2-3 times as often as the different-idea pairs, so a residual effect survives. Flagship 'time metaphor' example is one dominant vehicle plus a heavy tail, not two clusters. No human baseline in the original. 43 of 70+ models' generations reused; 15 models x 12 topics x 50 responses of their own.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed; authors say they do not resolve whether the Hivemind is real. Uses embedding similarity as the original did.
agent_relevance: Lowers confidence in claim K03 numbers (0.8 similarity) as an absolute; use a human or different-idea null when measuring our agent diversity.

source: Schaeffer et al. (2026) Reevaluating the Artificial Hivemind, Findings 9-10: prompt rewording and min-p
finding: Tests whether cheap inference-time changes break the Hivemind. Min-p's own authors' human evaluations show no advantage over top-p or basic sampling on quality, diversity or trade-off, so the original null result for min-p says little. Five prompt phrasings (creative adjective, unexpected domain, anti-modal 'consider what most models would write and choose differently', poet persona, quality anchor) were fixed ex ante and tested on 12 topics and 15 models, 50 samples each.
numbers: Every non-baseline phrasing raised effective rank at every scale. Poet persona strongest: effective rank 17.4 -> 28.9 (+66.1%) at one scale and 43.7 -> 120.2 (+175.0%) at another; pooled participation ratio more than tripled. Countable ideas per topic 3.34 baseline vs 3.99 (poet persona) and 3.97 (anti-modal). Authors note rewording moves embedding metrics more than the number of distinct ideas.
limits: Metaphor task only; embedding metrics; quality not resolved. Gains are in embedding spread, with a modest rise in distinct ideas.
agent_relevance: Persona and anti-modal prompts beat temperature on the same tasks. Supports a diverge operator that names and avoids the modal answer. Closes gap 6 partly.

source: Schapiro, Gladstone, Black, Ji (2026) Assessing the Creativity of Large Language Models: Testing, Limits, and New Frontiers
finding: Validity of DAT, CDAT, RAT and PACE as predictors of LLM creative achievement (gap 5). N=54 instruction-tuned models, 10 providers, six benchmarks. Creative achievement scores correlate with general capability up to 0.98, so they report raw validity and specificity (semi-partial after Arena Overall and MMLU-Pro). No test predicts all constructs.
numbers: DAT validity on creative writing: Arena CW +0.51, EQ-Bench +0.71, Mazur +0.66; specificity +0.41 and +0.49 on EQ-Bench and Mazur. Conditional DAT best for divergent thinking: NoveltyBench validity +0.63, specificity +0.60; Hivemind benchmark validity +0.25, specificity +0.10. Appropriateness facet CDAT-A on NoveltyBench validity -0.63, specificity -0.40. On LiveIdeaBench (scientific ideation, n=21) no existing test is significant (best specificity PACE +0.30 n.s.; DAT +0.28; CDAT +0.34). New DRAT test: validity +0.57 (p=0.008), specificity +0.52 (p=0.02). DAT and DRAT correlate only +0.14.
limits: Model-level correlations (not item-level), n=21-54 models, benchmark scores are partly LLM-judged, semantic scoring depends on embedding (GloVe, FastText, SBERT checked).
agent_relevance: Semantic-distance tests predict diversity benchmarks and creative writing but not science ideation. Do not use DAT alone as the agent open-mode metric; pair with a task benchmark and control for capability.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Assessing the Creativity of LLMs, Figure 1 and Section 1: trend over model release date
finding: Model-version drift (gap 4): across 54 models by public release date, construct-level z scores rose for creative writing and scientific ideation but fell for divergent thinking (diversity benchmarks).
numbers: Trend +1.22 z/year creative writing, +1.00 z/year scientific ideation, -0.47 z/year divergent thinking (OLS across models).
quote: Newer models are not automatically superior at divergent thinking
limits: Cross-sectional trend over mixed providers, not a within-model snapshot comparison; DT here means NoveltyBench and Hivemind diversity benchmarks, not DAT/AUT originality of single answers.
agent_relevance: Explains why GPT-4 84.56 vs GPT-4o 77.34 on DAT is not a fluke: post-training tends to reduce diversity. Pin snapshots in any comparison. Frontier 2026 DAT means are not reported here.

source: Schapiro, Sosa, Park, Varshney (2026) CreativityNeuro: Steering Language Model Weights to Improve Divergent Thinking and Reduce Mode Collapse
finding: Data-free contrastive weight steering on six open models (3B-14B). Beats prompting, decoding parameters and activation steering on DAT; human study (N=720 Prolific raters) on AUT and a 'Task Task' shows originality and surprise gains but lower utility on AUT.
numbers: DAT human percentile up to +14 points; mean percentile 94.1 (CN) vs 93.9 (activation steering) vs 87.9 (prompting) vs 87.8 (prompt-only steering). AUT originality avg d=+0.36 (4 of 6 models significant), surprise d=+0.43; Task Task originality d=+0.40 (Phi-14B +0.61, Qwen-14B +0.56), creativity d=+0.24. Activation steering did not transfer to AUT or Task Task. Baselines share top DAT words (galaxy, quasar, xylophone) across Llama, Phi and Qwen.
limits: Open small models only; weight edits are not available to a prompt-only agent; AUT utility fell (novelty-utility trade-off again).
agent_relevance: Confirms the cross-family shared-word problem and the originality-utility trade-off. Prompting gives most of the DAT gain at zero training cost.

source: Kumar, Vincentius, Jordan, Anderson (2025) Human Creativity in the Age of LLMs: Randomized Experiments on Divergent and Convergent Thinking (CHI 2025)
finding: Pre-registered extension to gap 9 with 1,100 participants in two experiments (AUT divergent, RAT convergent). AUT: 460 Prolific participants, 9,457 ideas, three arms (no LLM, LLM list of ideas, LLM list of strategies), then an unassisted test round. Strategy exposure lowered later originality and raised similarity of ideas.
numbers: Exposure-phase originality did not differ (H(2)=3.78, p=.151). Test phase originality differed (H(2)=9.14, p=.010): strategies arm below no-LLM, Dunn p=.009; ideas arm vs no-LLM p=1.000. Individual idea diversity (SBERT median cosine distance) test phase H(2)=7.71, p=.021, strategies vs no-LLM p=.017. Fluency exposure H(2)=8.57, p=.014 (strategies fewer ideas, p=.011), test fluency H(2)=1.14, p=.566. Group-level diversity exposure rounds p>.05. LLM ideas shown had mean originality 3.25 (1-5), about 0.5 above what participants wrote.
limits: Prolific crowd, 2-minute rounds, one delay, rater-scored originality; homogenization effect seen for strategies not for idea lists; post-hoc tests for creative flexibility not significant after correction (p=.052).
agent_relevance: Partial replication of Anderson 2024 at scale: LLM help does not raise later solo originality and may lower it. For a multiplayer agent, show ideas rather than prescribe strategies, and keep human-first idea rounds.

source: Carichon, Sharma, Girard, Rampa, Farnadi (2026) IDEAFix: Evaluation Framework for Creative Defixation Prompting in LLMs
finding: 81 design briefs expanded into 567 task variants, 25 prompting strategies from creativity methods (SCAMPER, TRIZ, C-K, design thinking, brainstorming, AI-specific). All method prompts beat the control on novelty by t-test, but short prompts urging 'wild, bold, unconventional, even absurd' and breaking usual categories beat the complex method-based prompts. Fixation and cross-model homogenization persist.
numbers: Best prompts gave roughly +10% to +41% on novelty and rarity metrics depending on measure and top-5 vs mean (figure labels e.g. +12.14% SCAMPER, +30.92% scenario, +41.36% AI-specific top-5). Brief type changed results: some brief types gave higher novelty but lower fluency and diversity; service briefs lowest on all. Grok and Llama produced more novel outputs than other models.
limits: Brief-level metrics by embedding and rarity, LLM models mixed, percentages read from a figure and appendix tables; no human ratings in the main text I read.
agent_relevance: Complex creativity methods as scaffolds do not beat a short explicit divergence instruction. Weighs against adding SCAMPER/TRIZ style operators for gains in novelty (gap 1).

source: Liu, Dubova, Conklin, Harada, Griffiths (2026) Assessing the Effect of Cross-Domain Mapping on Creativity in Humans and Large Language Models
finding: Forced random-source analogies as a divergence scaffold. 140 humans and 7 LLMs (o3, Claude-Sonnet-4, gpt-4o, gemini-2.5-pro and others) designed products from a random source or from a user need; 1,002 raters judged ideas. Humans gained from almost any source; LLMs made more original ideas at baseline but showed no overall gain, gaining only when the source was far in semantic distance and only for the highest-rated LLMs.
numbers: Humans N=140 (70 per product per condition), raters N=1,002 (about 10% excluded for failed catch trials). More distant source-target pairs produced more original ideas for both. Humans transferred surface features; LLMs transferred structural and functional properties.
limits: Product design only; judged startup-pitch originality; effort differs between crowd workers and LLMs (authors say LLMs can be told to try less).
agent_relevance: A random-remote-source step helps only when the source is far; supports sampling a distant seed only for strong models, not a blanket analogy step.

source: Ismayilzada, Luchini, Gokce, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Laverghetta, van der Plas, Beaty (2026) Large Language Models Align with the Human Brain during Creative Thinking (COLM 2026)
finding: fMRI from 170 participants doing the AUT compared with LLM representations (270M-72B) by RSA in default mode and frontoparietal networks. Alignment rises with model size (default mode only) and with idea originality. A creativity-optimized Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct keeps alignment with high-creativity responses; a reasoning-trained variant shows negative alignment to high-creativity responses.
numbers: N=170 humans; models 270M to 72B; numeric effect sizes not read beyond the abstract and introduction.
limits: Read abstract and introduction only for the post-training result; correlational; representation geometry is not behaviour.
agent_relevance: A hint that reasoning-style training moves a model away from the neural geometry of creative thought; keep reasoning steps in the converge phase, not the diverge phase.

source: Khan and Wester (2026) Seeing the Hivemind: A Consensus-Aware Interaction Technique for Mitigating AI Homogenization (Semantic Repulsion Technique)
finding: Test of 'sample what is common, then ban it' for gap 6. SRT samples the model K=12 times, finds the consensus centroid and repeated phrases, then generates away from them as negative concepts. Computational semantic diversity rose 85-167% and consensus phrases fell 43-95%. Small user study with 16 regular AI-creativity users: usefulness and coherence up; originality and coherence positively correlated (+.40 to +.67).
numbers: 16 participants; 68.8% willing to use SRT-Strong for multiple tasks vs 18.8% for baselines; percentage ranges from the abstract as extracted.
limits: Pilot, N=16, writing tasks, self-built metrics; no AUT/DAT.
agent_relevance: Supports 'sample, find the modal answer and repeated phrases, then forbid them' as an O-diverge operator with 12 samples; cost is K extra calls.

source: Beyond the Hivemind: Escaping LLM Homogeneity via Meta-Persona Anchoring and Sequential Temperature Scaling (2026, author names not captured)
finding: Two-stage method: model first self-selects an idiosyncratic persona, then samples with top-p filtering followed by extreme temperature (T up to 4.0). On Infinity-Chat with open models under 20B, average pairwise cosine fell from about 0.85 to 0.65, with most questions under 0.7. Baseline above 0.8 in all cases; one reasoning model started at IRCS 0.880.
numbers: IRCS 0.85 -> 0.65; baseline top-p 0.9 no persona above 0.8 for all models; coherence reported as high (judge details not read).
limits: Small open models, no human evaluation, coherence validated by LLM judge; persona and temperature changed together so the active ingredient is unknown.
agent_relevance: Persona anchoring plus temperature reduces embedding similarity but combines two changes. Treat as weak evidence.

source: Crossref records and PsycNet pages for Runco (2008) Commentary: Divergent thinking is not synonymous with creativity (doi 10.1037/1931-3896.2.2.93) and Acar, Runco, Park (2020) meta-analysis of explicit instructions (doi 10.1037/aca0000256)
finding: Attempt to close gaps 2 and 7. Crossref confirms both records exist (Runco May 2008; Acar et al. Feb 2020, titled 'What should people be told when they take a divergent thinking test? A meta-analytic review of explicit instructions for divergent thinking'). PsycNet returned only a loading shell and Taylor and Francis returned HTTP 403, so no text or numbers could be read.
numbers: None extracted. Existing b23 (g .24-.27) stays unverified.
limits: Paywalled; not opened. Do not treat as evidence of content.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 7 remain open; need institutional access or an open preprint.
